intro: These six span twenty kilometres of Toronto, several outings rather than one afternoon. The oldest is Zhelevo, a red oak in Etobicoke that predates European settlement of the Humber River, saved when the city bought and demolished the house beside it. The official tree, in Kew Gardens, has one limb sagging to the grass. A coronation oak from 1937 anchors a ring of maples on the waterfront, Big Red holds a corner in Long Branch, a Turkish hazel survives a private nut farm, and six maples in Lambton were planted by grieving mothers on Remembrance Day, 1919.
meta_description: Toronto's oldest tree is Zhelevo, a 300-year red oak the city bought a house to save. Six heritage trees, from Kew Gardens to a WWI remembrance planting.
question_meta: Toronto's oldest tree is Zhelevo, a roughly 300-year red oak in Etobicoke the city bought a house to save. Where it stands, and five more to see.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Toronto is Zhelevo, a red oak on Coral Gable Drive in Etobicoke, at roughly three hundred years old with an honest band running from 250 to 320. It predates the European settlement of the Humber River area, which began in 1793, and stood near the old Toronto Carrying Place Trail between Lake Ontario and Lake Simcoe. Its trunk measures nearly five metres round and its crown, at 24 metres, used to tower over the private house beside it, until Toronto City Council voted in 2020 to buy that property and demolish the house instead, after a public campaign of more than 1,300 donors got there first. The city is building a public parkette on the lot now, due to open in spring 2027; until then the tree is visible from the street rather than walk-up. Toronto's official tree, the red oak in Kew Gardens, is close behind at roughly 220 years, a title the city gave it in 2022 for its own reasons rather than for age: its trunk measures 5.3 metres round, the crown reaches roughly 36 metres, and arborists read a diameter of 169 centimetres as an age of about 220 years, with an honest band running from 200 to 260. Nobody has cored either tree, so both bands are the answer rather than a hedge.
question_context: Ontario has no government register of remarkable trees. What it has instead is the Ontario Heritage Tree Program run by Forests Ontario, a nomination-based designation, and that is where all six trees on this page come from; each was then checked against independent sources, a city page, a local historical society or a newspaper. Most ages here come off a tape measure and an assumed growth rate, with three exceptions: the King's Oak was planted on 12 May 1937 and the Lambton Park maples on 11 November 1919, both birthdays known to the day, and Zhelevo's age follows several newspapers' converged estimate of roughly 300 years rather than the register's own older figure of 250. Two figures on this page disagree and both are recorded rather than reconciled: Forests Canada puts Big Red at 24 metres tall, a 2024 local report at 33. Two cautions about precision: the five heritage trees in Echo Valley Park share a single map coordinate, which is why the Turkish hazel here is marked approximate, and the six Lambton Park maples share one register coordinate the same way.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Toronto?
faq.a: Zhelevo, a red oak on Coral Gable Drive in Etobicoke, at roughly 300 years old with a band running from 250 to 320. It predates European settlement of the Humber River area and was saved when the city bought and demolished the house beside it in 2020. Toronto's official tree, the red oak in Kew Gardens, is close behind at roughly 220 years.

faq.q: Can I see them all in one walk?
faq.a: No, and it would be a long day to try. Zhelevo is in Etobicoke near the Humber River, Kew Gardens is in the Beaches, Coronation Park is on the waterfront by the CNE grounds, Big Red is in Long Branch, the Turkish hazel is in Echo Valley Park in Islington and the Lambton Park maples stand nearby in Lambton, which together span roughly twenty kilometres end to end. Each is a short walk from transit, so treat them as separate outings.

Yes, all six, though Zhelevo is currently viewable from the street rather than walk-up: the city is building a public parkette around it, due to open in spring 2027. Every other tree stands on public ground, and Coronation Park and the Long Branch corner are open at all hours. The Lambton Park maples stand on the school's street frontage and are viewable from the public sidewalk without entering the schoolyard.

faq.q: Is the tree in Echo Valley Park easy to find?
faq.a: No. George Corsan's surviving nut trees in that park are all on the heritage register under a single shared map coordinate, so the last part is a short hunt among them, and no published source says which is which. Nobody has reported a sighting since the 2017 nomination either. If you find it, tell us and we will fix the page.

faq.q: Why are six trees counted as one entry?
faq.a: The Lambton Park maples, two silver and four Norway, were all planted the same day for the same twelve names and share one register coordinate rather than six surveyed positions. We list them as a single collectible point rather than pretend to six separate pins we cannot back up.

trees.name: The Kew Gardens Red Oak

location.address: Kew Gardens, 2075 Queen St E, Toronto

trees.story:
Toronto has an official tree, and this is it. The city gave the title in 2022 to a northern red oak in Kew Gardens, a trunk 5.3 metres round under a crown reaching about 36 metres, with one long limb that sags all the way down to the grass.

Arborists read its start off a diameter of 169 centimetres and put it at roughly 220 years, with a band running from about 200 to 260. Nobody has cored it, so that band is the honest answer: it may or may not predate the founding of the town that became Toronto.

Everything else on this corner arrived afterwards. Joseph Williams farmed the land from the 1850s and ran amusement grounds beneath these branches; the city bought the 8.4 hectares in 1907. The creeks that once ran down to the lake here were culverted while the oak stood over them. Forests Ontario designated it a heritage tree in 2021, and a Heritage Toronto plaque went up in May 2023, which is late recognition for something that was already large when the first houses in the Beaches were built.

A native plant garden now grows under the low limb. Stand beside it and the limb is at shoulder height, which is not how most people expect to meet a 36 metre tree.
verified_sources: Ontario Heritage Tree Program (Forests Canada/OUFC) register entry HT-2021-255-266
trees.access: Free, public park, open daylight hours
trees.transport: Streetcar (504 King or 501 Queen) to Kew Beach; Woodbine subway station + 15 min walk
trees.how_to_recognise: The biggest tree in the park, with one long low limb sagging all the way to the grass over a native plant garden. A Heritage Toronto plaque stands beside it.

trees.name: The King's Oak

location.address: Coronation Park, Lake Shore Blvd W, Toronto

trees.story:
On 12 May 1937, while George VI was being crowned in London, Toronto put an oak in the ground on the lakeshore and planted about 150 more trees around it before the day was out.

The oak is the centre of the arrangement. Around it run concentric rings of silver maples, the Empire Circle, one ring for each dominion and colony of an empire that has since stopped existing. The rings are still there. So is the oak, 89 years on, an ordinary pedunculate oak carrying a considerable amount of ceremony: a stone and plaque beside it, dedicated by Justice John A. Hope and unveiled by Sir William Mulock in August 1938.

Then it happened again. On 6 May 2023, for the coronation of Charles III, the city planted a companion oak next to the first one and added a second plaque. Eighty-six years apart, the same gesture, the same species, the same patch of grass. The second planting is also the reason we know the first tree is still standing.

This is the youngest tree on this page and the only one whose birthday is known to the day; every other age here comes off a tape measure around a trunk. Coronation Park has since been restored in phases, and the first phase went to this oak and its circle of maples.
verified_sources: Ontario Heritage Tree Program (Forests Canada/OUFC) register entry HT-2015-49-116
trees.access: Free, public waterfront park, open at all hours
trees.transport: Streetcar 509/511 to Exhibition Loop, then 10 min walk; or Exhibition GO station
trees.how_to_recognise: The single oak at the centre of the concentric rings of silver maples, with a stone and plaque beside it. A second, much younger oak was planted next to it in 2023.

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.name: Big Red

location.address: Corner of Long Branch Ave. and Park Blvd, beside the Long Branch Cenotaph

trees.story:
The Long Branch Hotel burned down in 1958. The oak beside it did not, and it is still on the corner.

Big Red is a northern red oak at Long Branch Avenue and Park Boulevard, named by the neighbourhood for what it does in October. Diameter measurements put its start in the late 1810s; Forests Canada rounds that to about 200 years and the early 1800s, which is close enough agreement to work with. Its height is less settled. Forests Canada records 24 metres, a 2024 local report says 33, and neither explains how it was measured, so both figures are on the record and neither has won.

In the late 1800s it stood near a fountain in the grounds of the Long Branch Grove and Resort, a lakeside destination Torontonians came out to by train. The resort went. The hotel went. The streets arrived. In 1933 the cenotaph went up beside the oak, and the tree has stood next to the names of three wars ever since, which is the reason to come in November rather than the reason to come in October.

Forests Ontario made it Long Branch's first heritage tree in April 2018, listed at 200 years. It is by some distance the oldest thing on that corner.

best_time.label: late October, when the crown turns the deep red it is named for

verified_sources: Ontario Heritage Tree Program (Forests Canada/OUFC) register entry HT-2017-211-233
trees.access: Free, public memorial park beside the Long Branch Cenotaph, open at all hours
trees.transport: Long Branch GO station or 501 Long Branch streetcar loop, 10 min walk
trees.how_to_recognise: The large oak on the corner beside the Long Branch cenotaph. It is by a distance the oldest thing standing there.

trees.name: Corsan's Turkish Hazel

location.address: Echo Valley Park, off Wingrove Hill near 1124 Kipling Avenue

trees.story:
George Hebden Corsan was an internationally known swimmer and a health food evangelist, and he spent forty years proving that nut trees would grow in Ontario. This is one of the trees that proved it.

Corsan bought twelve acres here across 1911 and 1912 and turned them into a nut farm, eventually cultivating more than 400 varieties and collecting the name the Nut Man of Islington. Metropolitan Toronto bought the land in 1959 and made it Echo Valley Park, which is the only reason a private obsession is now something anyone can walk through.

The Turkish hazel is one of five of his nut trees on the heritage register, alongside a hican, a black walnut and two more walnuts. The register recorded this one at 100 years old in 2017 and dates the planting loosely to the 1900s, without tying it to Corsan's own arrival, so early last century is as close as the evidence gets. A 1971 survey by the University of Toronto's Shade Tree Research Laboratory listed Turkish hazel among the nut species still growing on the site, which is the second account standing behind the register entry.

Two honest gaps. All five trees share a single map pin, so the last part of the walk is a short hunt. And nobody has published a sighting since the 2017 nomination. If you find it, or work out which of the five is which, tell us.

trees.access: Free, public park (Etobicoke Parks System since 1959), multiple entrances off Kipling Avenue and Wingrove Hill
trees.transport: Islington subway station, then bus along Kipling/Burnhamthorpe, roughly 15-20 min total
trees.how_to_recognise: Hard. All five of Corsan's nut trees share one map pin, so expect a short hunt, and nobody has published which of the five is which. If you work it out, tell us.

trees.name: The Lambton Park Remembrance Trees
trees.species: Silver Maple and Norway Maple (Acer saccharinum and Acer platanoides)

location.address: Lambton Park Community School, 50 Bernice Crescent, Toronto

trees.story:
Twelve local men from this part of Toronto died in the First World War. Six trees went into the ground for them on 11 November 1919, the very first Remembrance Day, planted on the lawn in front of Lambton Park Community School.

Two silver maples and four Norway maples went in with a silver-plated shovel, because the two men invited to turn the first sod, Princes Edward and Albert of England, could not make the crossing. The mothers of the fallen planted the trees themselves instead.

For most of a century the planting sat unmarked. Bonita Nelson, a descendant of two of the twelve, Reginald Gage and Sydney Moyle, nominated the trees for heritage status in 2016, and a plaque inside the school now carries all twelve names.

The register places the six trees along the school's Bernice Crescent frontage, reachable from the public sidewalk without stepping onto school grounds. The last confirmed sighting is the 2016 nomination itself, so ask at the school if you want certainty before you go, and tell us what you find. A tree planted for twelve names deserves better than an unconfirmed pin.
trees.access: Free. The six trees stand at the front of Lambton Park Community School facing Bernice Crescent, on the street-facing frontage, viewable and reachable from the public sidewalk without entering school grounds.
trees.transport: TTC bus 40 (Junction-Dundas West) or 79 (Scarlett Rd) on Dundas St West at Scarlett Road, short walk to Bernice Crescent.
trees.how_to_recognise: Six maples in a row along the school's Bernice Crescent frontage, two silver and four Norway. No published photo distinguishes one from another; all six commemorate the same twelve names.

trees.name: Zhelevo, the Coral Gable Drive Red Oak

location.address: 76 Coral Gable Drive, Etobicoke, Toronto, Ontario

trees.access: Free once open. The City of Toronto bought the private lot specifically to save this tree and is building a public parkette on it; as of the City's own July 2026 project update the house has been demolished and construction is underway, with opening projected Spring 2027. Until then the tree (which visibly dwarfs the former house from the street) is viewable from Coral Gable Drive but the lot itself is a construction site, not yet open ground.
trees.transport: Residential Etobicoke street near the Humber River; no specific TTC bus route to the door was confirmed by this pass. Reachable by bus from Islington or Kipling stations on the Bloor-Danforth subway line.
trees.story:
In 2020 Toronto's city council voted to buy a private house on Coral Gable Drive, not to live in it, but to tear it down and save the oak growing beside it. Locals call the tree Zhelevo, after a Macedonian village, and more than 1,300 donors helped fund the years-long campaign that got the city to act before a developer could.

The oak predates the city itself. At roughly three centuries old, it stood here before European settlement reached the Humber River in 1793, part of an oak savannah that once lined the old Toronto Carrying Place trail between Lake Ontario and Lake Simcoe. Its trunk runs nearly five metres round and its crown, at 24 metres, used to dwarf the house that stood beside it.

That house is gone now. The city is building a public parkette on the lot, due to open in spring 2027, and until then the oak is visible from the street rather than walk-up, towering over a construction site instead of a front lawn. It has already survived roughly three hundred years of whatever Toronto threw at it. A couple more waiting for a gate to open is nothing.
